newsitem.title: USA: Oregon sees revenue boost of $145 mln to $9.4 bln.
newsitem.headline: Oregon sees revenue boost of $145 mln to $9.4 bln.

text.p: Oregon lawmakers will have $9.4 billion to spend in the 1997-1999 budget period, an increase of $145.8 million from previous projections in March, the state's Economic and Revenue Forecast said on Thursday.
The increase was attributed to stronger-than-expected corporate tax revenues, a boost in lottery revenues due to accounting changes, and interest on the general fund, state officials said.

The May forecast is important because state offices base their budgets on these figures, which are known as close of session forecasts, according to Office of Economic Analysis Senior Economist David Griffiths.

Lottery revenues were up $48 million, of which $27.1 million were due to technical changes. Corporate tax revenues are seen at $619.5 million, but this does not include an anticipated $160.5 million which may be returned to taxpayers, state officials said.

Under state law, lawmakers will not be able to spend all of the added revenues. The so-called "kicker" law requires tax income to be returned to corporate and personal taxpayers when revenues exceeds estimates by more than 2.0 percent.
State economists said 1997's first quarter showed signs the economy was slowing, with the construction sector slowing significantly.
But the economists said growth in the state's key high technology sector remains strong, and they predicted continued personal income and job growth.

Total personal income, adjusted for inflation, is expected to rise by 4.6 percent this year and 3.2 percent in 1998. Per capita income is seen increasing from $22,837 in 1996 to $24,924 in 1998, according to the state analysis.
Non-farm employment is forecast to increase 3.5 percent this year and 2.3 percent in 1998. The state's population is expected to grow 1.7 percent in both 1997 and 1998, the forecast said.
